readerTitle: Same sales, same profit. Why does one restaurant hold five times the stock?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (레스토랑 두 곳, IT 유지보수 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 재고는 선반 위에 쌓인 현금이다. 그 현금이 1년에 몇 번 매출로 돌아오는지(회전율)를 보면, 같은 이익을 내는 두 사업의 건강 상태가 전혀 다르게 보인다.
misconception: 이익률이 같고 재고가 떨어지지 않으면 재고를 얼마나 쌓아 두든 상관없다. 회전율은 높을수록 무조건 좋다.

sources.text: 관리회계·재무분석의 표준 개념 (재고회전율 = 매출원가 ÷ 평균 재고, 재고일수 = 365 ÷ 회전율)

factChecks.note: IT 회사 계산: $240,000 ÷ $80,000 = 3회, 365 ÷ 3 ≈ 121.7일(약 4개월). 카드에는 "about four months"로 적었습니다.
softwareNote의 '물류 대행 창고가 오래 머문 재고에 보관료를 부과한다'는 일반적 관행으로 서술했습니다. 특정 업체명·요율은 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.

cards.title: Same sales, same profit. Why does one restaurant hold five times the stock?
body: Two restaurants on the same street each spend $300,000 a year on food and drink. Their menus earn similar margins. Their profits look alike.
Walk into the storerooms, though, and they look nothing alike. One has $10,000 of stock on its shelves. The other has $50,000.

image.label: Two storerooms side by side, one sparse, one packed
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽은 선반이 가볍게 채워진 작은 창고, 오른쪽은 와인 상자와 식자재 박스가 천장까지 쌓인 창고. 두 문 앞에 같은 크기의 동전 더미를 놓아 이익이 같다는 점을 암시. 실제 브랜드 로고·라벨은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Which restaurant is in better shape?
body: Restaurant A buys fresh several times a week and keeps about $10,000 of stock. Restaurant B buys in bulk, keeps a deep wine cellar and holds about $50,000. B's owner says, "We never run out."
Profits are about equal. Which business would you rather own?

options.text: They're equal. Same sales, same profit
options.feedback: The profit statement says they're equal. But B needs $40,000 more cash to earn the same profit, cash that could pay down debt or fund a new oven.

options.text: Restaurant B. It never runs out and buys at bulk prices
options.feedback: Never running out has real value, and bulk prices can help. But you pay for that safety with cash that sits still, plus storage space and spoilage risk.

options.text: Restaurant A. Its stock turns back into sales much faster
options.feedback: Right. A earns the same profit with a fifth of the money tied up. The next card shows how to measure that speed.

cards.title: How often does the stock come back as sales?
body: Divide what each restaurant spends on food and drink in a year by the stock it holds. A empties and refills its shelves **30 times** a year. B does it **6 times**.

cards.title: Inventory turnover
body: **Inventory turnover** is how many times a year you sell through the stock you hold. Take what your sold goods cost you over a year, then divide by the average value of stock on hand.
Flip it around and you get **days on hand**: 365 divided by turnover. It tells you how long a typical item waits before a customer pays for it.
Use cost, not selling price, on both sides, so you compare like with like.

image.label: Coins cycling from shelf to register and back
image.brief: 순환 화살표 인포그래픽. "Cash" → "Stock on shelf" → "Sale" → 다시 "Cash". 왼쪽 원은 빠르게 30바퀴 도는 느낌(모션 라인 많음), 오른쪽 원은 느리게 6바퀴. 각 원 아래 "30× a year", "6× a year" 라벨.

cards.softwareNote: An online store runs the same math. Fulfillment warehouses often charge storage fees each month, and more for items that sit a long time, so slow stock costs you rent as well as cash.

cards.title: Every turn brings the money back.
body: Each time stock sells, the money you spent on it returns, along with your margin. Then you spend it again.
For every $1 sitting on A's shelves, A sells $30 worth of food (at cost) in a year. For every $1 on B's shelves, B sells just $6. Same menu margins, but A's money works five times harder.
Slow stock adds quieter costs too: shelf space, spoiled produce, wine that gets damaged or goes missing.

cards.title: Service firms hold stock too.
body: An IT support company sells its time, yet keeps spare laptops, cables and parts for client repairs. A building maintenance firm keeps filters and fittings in its vans. Anything bought before a customer pays for it is inventory.
And one number for the whole business can hide a lot. B's fresh produce may turn every few days while its cellar barely moves. **Measure turnover by category**, and the slow corner usually jumps out.

image.label: Van and shelf of spare parts with day counters
image.brief: 정비 회사 창고 선반 일러스트. 부품 상자마다 작은 꼬리표: "Cables · 9 days", "Laptops · 40 days", "Old printer parts · 300 days". 마지막 꼬리표에 먼지 표현. 실제 제조사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Faster isn't always better.
body: Turnover rises when you hold less stock. Push it too far and you run out of the dish everyone ordered, or pay more for small, frequent deliveries.
Comparisons only work within an industry. A florist should turn stock far faster than a jeweler. That doesn't make the jeweler badly run.
Use the average stock over the year, not one snapshot. A count taken right after a big delivery makes any business look slow.

cards.title: Now it's an IT support firm.
body: Your firm installs about $240,000 of parts a year for business clients. You keep $80,000 of spares on hand, so stock turns three times a year, about four months on the shelf. Several clients pay you to fix problems within hours.
You want to free up cash. What do you do?

options.text: Cut every spare part to the bare minimum
options.feedback: Turnover jumps, but a missing part can break a same-day repair promise. You'd save cash and lose the clients who pay for speed.

options.text: Check turnover part by part, clear out slow items, keep fast-moving critical spares
options.feedback: You release the cash stuck in parts nobody uses and keep the ones that protect your service promise. It takes an afternoon with the records.

options.text: Take the supplier's bulk discount to lower your parts cost
options.feedback: A lower price helps margins, but buying more at once ties up even more cash. It only pays if those parts actually sell quickly.

cards.title: Stock is cash on a shelf. Count how fast it comes back.
body: Two businesses can earn the same profit while one needs far more money to do it. Inventory turnover shows which one.
**Try it today:** take last year's cost of goods sold and divide it by your average stock value. Then do it again for your slowest category.
